fetched_contents.text: Reading in a Foreign Language October 2007, Volume 19, No. 2 ISSN 1539-0578 pp. 120-136 The effects of synonymy on second-language vocabulary learning Stuart Webb Koran Women's Junior College Japan Abstract This article examines the effects of synonymy (i.e., learning words with and without high-frequency synonyms that were known to the learners) on word knowledge in a study of 84 Japanese students learning English. It employed 10 tests measuring 5 aspects of word knowledge (orthography, paradigmatic association, syntagmatic association, meaning and form, and grammatical functions) to assess learning. Both receptive and productive tests were used to measure each aspect of vocabulary knowledge. The participants encountered target words in 2 learning conditions: glossed sentences and word pairs. The results showed that the learners had significantly higher scores for the words that had known synonyms on productive knowledge as measured using syntagmatic association and paradigmatic association tests and on receptive knowledge as measured using an orthography test. The findings indicate that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words that do not have known synonyms. Keywords: incidental learning, synonymy, vocabulary knowledge, word pairs, glossed sentences Very little research has investigated the effects of synonymy on vocabulary learning. Higa (1963) found that learning two synonyms at one time is more difficult than learning two unrelated words, and synonymy has been listed as one of several factors that can make words more difficult to learn (Laufer, 1990). However, to my knowledge, no studies have examined the difficulty of learning a synonym for a known word versus that of learning a non-synonym. This is surprising because learning the synonyms of known words is a very common occurrence in vocabulary learning, and intuitively and logically, learning a synonym would be easier than learning a non-synonym. It is understandable, however, because students tend to learn the majority of synonyms in the later stages of vocabulary learning, and researchers are more focused on the earlier stages of vocabulary learning, which are critical to language acquisition. Moreover, in the classroom, teachers and learners might be more motivated to teach and learn words that convey new information rather than teaching and learning forms that convey information similar to what learners already know. The similarity between synonyms, however, may make learning the synonyms of known words easier than learning words without known synonyms. Overlaps in collocation, syntagmatic and paradigmatic associations, grammatical functions, and meaning and form between synonyms may help to facilitate vocabulary acquisition. http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl Webb: The effects of synonymy on second-language vocabulary learning 121 The present study was designed to determine whether learning synonyms for known second- language (L2) words is easier than learning non-synonyms. The reason for this was not to advocate the teaching of synonyms but rather to improve our understanding of the vocabulary acquisition process. If words with known synonyms are learned more easily than words without known synonyms, learning new words would become easier as a learner's vocabulary size increases because more and more words are likely to have known synonyms. Vocabulary difficulty would thus be affected by the amount of prior learning. Learners with larger vocabularies would be able to learn words more easily than learners with smaller vocabularies because increased vocabulary knowledge would help to facilitate learning. Literature Review In the only study that investigated the effects of synonymy on vocabulary learning, Higa (1963) found that pairs of synonyms took longer to learn than pairs of unrelated words. The results suggested that learners are more likely to confuse words that are similar in meaning than words that do not have close semantic links. Higa (1963, 1965) reported that the closer the semantic relationship between words, the more difficult it may be to learn the words in a set. Studies by Tinkham (1993) and Waring (1997) also indicate that learning sets of semantically related words is more difficult than learning words that are not linked by meaning. Together, these studies suggest that learning synonyms together may reduce the likelihood of acquisition. While this is a very useful finding, it may not apply to the way in which synonyms are usually learned. Teachers are unlikely to teach pairs of unknown synonyms together for the simple reason that it is confusing for learners, as Higa's research suggests, and learners are unlikely to learn synonyms together because they may lack the motivation to learn two words that convey similar information. Instead, a synonym for a known word may be easier to learn in the later stages of vocabulary learning. At present, no research appears to have investigated the difficulty of learning the synonyms of known words versus learning non-synonyms. Laufer (1990) reported that synonymy is one of seven interlexical factors that can reduce the chances of vocabulary acquisition. She gave two reasons that synonyms may be more difficult to learn than other words. First, learners often make mistakes using synonyms because some of them may be substituted effectively in some contexts but not in others. For example, strong and powerful have similar meanings, but usually tea is only strong, and engines may be powerful but are rarely strong. This is an important point and demonstrates that some synonyms might be more difficult to learn than others because synonyms with similar meanings do not always have the same collocates. Published in final edited form as: J Exp Psychol Gen. 2015 Feb 16;144(2):410–431. doi: 10.1037/xge0000051 Abstract Learning often affects future learning and memory for previously learned information by exerting either facilitation or interference effects. Several theoretical accounts of interference effects have been proposed, each making different developmental predictions. This research examines interference effects across development, with the goal of better understanding mechanisms of interference and of memory development. Preschool-aged children and adults participated in a three-phased associative learning paradigm containing stimuli that were either unique or repeated across phases. Both age groups demonstrated interference effects, but only for repeated items. Whereas proactive interference effects were comparable across age groups, retroactive interference reached catastrophic-like levels in children. Additionally, retroactive interference increased in adults when contextual differences between phases were minimized (Experiment 2), and decreased in adults who were more successful at encoding repeated pairs of stimuli during a training phase (Experiment 3). These results are discussed with respect to theories of memory and memory development. ---------------------------------------- There is much work suggesting that learning and memory interact, in that previously acquired knowledge affects acquisition of new knowledge (Krascum & Andrews, 1998; Murphy & Allopenna, 1994) and newly acquired knowledge affects memory for established knowledge (Roediger & Marsh, 2005). In some cases this interaction is facilitative. For example, expertise in a particular domain often benefits memory for information within that domain (Chi, Glaser, & Rees, 1982; Guida, Gobet, Tardieu, & Nicolas, 2012). Previous knowledge may also assist category learning (Murphy & Allopenna, 1994) and learning of causal relations (Griffiths, Sobel, Tenenbaum, & Gopnik, 2011). Similarly, seminal work by Ebbinghaus demonstrated savings effects, in which unconscious memory for previous learning facilitates later learning of the same information (Nelson, 1985). At the same time, interactions between learning and memory can also produce interference effects: under some conditions, memory for previously learned information attenuates learning of new information (i.e., proactive interference, or PI), whereas under other conditions, learning of new information attenuates memory for previously learned information (i.e., retroactive interference, or RI). For example, a professor may experience PI when finding it difficult to learn students' names at the beginning of each semester, as he or she has taught many students previously. At the same time, RI may affect the professor's ability to recall the name of a particular student from a previous semester, as he or she has since learned the names of other students. Interference effects can be relatively benign, as in this example, but can also be very disruptive for learning and memory. As discussed below, resistance to PI and RI and developmental changes in these effects may provide important information about mechanisms of interference and about memory development. The current research examines developmental differences in interference with the goal of better understanding mechanisms of proactive and retroactive interference effects and of memory development. Researchers have studied interference effects experimentally for over a century, producing a wealth of theories and insights into the mechanisms of learning and memory (see Anderson & Neely, 1996; Wixted, 2004, for reviews). Traditionally, susceptibility to PI has been related to the integrity of executive function, in that executive control processes help to minimize PI effects (see Anderson & Neely, 1996; Jonides & Nee, 2006, for reviews). Some researchers have suggested that susceptibility to RI is also a function of executive control, in that executive processes create RI by inhibiting memories during retrieval that are not currently relevant (Anderson, 2003; Bjork, 1989). Other work, however, suggests that susceptibility to RI may be modulated by the integrity of memory traces sub-served by encoding and consolidation processes (Humphreys, Bain, & Pike, 1989; McClelland, McNaughton, & O'Reilly, 1995). Studying interference effects in different developmental populations, in which processes of executive control and memory formation are known to differ, can shed light on the mechanistic underpinnings of interference, as well as inform our understanding of memory development. We will return to this issue in the section on memory development. A standard way of experimentally examining PI and RI effects would be to present a learning task X (e.g., Study List 1) followed by a learning task Y (e.g., Study List 2). PI is typically defined as attenuation of learning on List 2 that is not attributable to fatigue or other non-memory factors (see Anderson & Neely, 1996; Jonides & Nee, 2006; Kail, 2002, for reviews). Similarly, RI is typically defined as attenuation of memory for information presented in List 1 following learning of List 2 (assuming that attenuation is not attributable to fatigue or other non-memory factors; see Wixted, 2004 for a review). fetched_contents.text: "The Effect of Retrieval Practice on Vocabulary Learning for Children w" by Casey Krauss Reimer The Effect of Retrieval Practice on Vocabulary Learning for Children who are Deaf or Hard of Hearing Abstract The goal of the current study was to determine if students who are deaf or hard of hearing (d/hh) would learn more new vocabulary words through the use of retrieval practice than repeated exposure (repeated study). No studies to date have used this cognitive strategy—retrieval practice—with children who are d/hh. Previous studies have shown that children with hearing loss struggle with learning vocabulary words. This deficit can negatively affect language development, reading outcomes, and overall academic success. Few studies have investigated specific interventions to address the poor vocabulary development for children with hearing loss. The current study investigated retrieval practice as a potentially effective strategy to increase word-learning for children who are d/hh and who use spoken language. It was found that children with hearing loss recalled a greater number of new vocabulary words when using retrieval practice than repeated exposure after a two day retention interval. This study also examined factors that influence whether a child remembers or forgets a word after a retention interval. Children who did not have an additional diagnosis recalled more words than children with an additional diagnosis. Children who were more efficient learners—took fewer trials to learn the word—recalled more words than children who were less efficient learners. Mechanisms explaining negative effects of synonym generation

The evidence points to several theoretical pathways by which synonym generation can hurt recall: interference, reduced attention to target words, and confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval. First, interference theory explains why similar memories compete and make recall harder. The core idea is that previously learned information can interfere with new learning or with retrieval of previously learned information, either proactively or retroactively. This framework is directly relevant because synonym generation introduces semantically related material, which can create interference effects when the generated synonym overlaps with the target word’s meaning or with other previously learned vocabulary. The evidence also notes that interference effects can be disruptive and that susceptibility to interference can vary with age and memory processes, suggesting that synonym generation may interfere more when learners have less executive control or weaker encoding/consolidation processes [N2-R1][N2-F2].

Second, overgeneralization or overlearning can be a negative mechanism. The evidence emphasizes that synonymy can be difficult to learn because synonyms are semantically related and may be confused with one another. In the literature review, Webb notes that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words without known synonyms, but also that synonymy can be a source of difficulty because learners may confuse similar words, especially when they are closely related in meaning [N1-F1]. The review also points out that synonymy is one of several interlexical factors that can reduce vocabulary acquisition, partly because synonyms may be substituted effectively in some contexts but not in others, which can lead to overgeneralization of usage [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that synonym generation can hurt recall not only because of interference, but because learners may overlearn or generalize patterns that do not generalize correctly across contexts.

Third, reduced attention to target words during generation appears plausible. The evidence suggests that when learners are asked to generate synonyms, they may shift attention away from the target word itself. The review notes that synonymy is often learned as a later-stage phenomenon, and that teachers are unlikely to teach pairs of unknown synonyms together because it is confusing for learners [N1-F1]. This implies that synonym generation may be less effective when it is not paired with explicit attention to the target word’s meaning, form, or usage. In addition, the comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure suggests that retrieval practice can be more effective than repeated exposure because it forces learners to engage with the material actively, which implies that passive or synonym-generating tasks may fail to maintain attention at the target word level [N3-F3].

Fourth, confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval is a central mechanism. The literature review explicitly states that learners are more likely to confuse words that are similar in meaning than words that do not have close semantic links [N1-F1]. This directly supports the idea that synonym generation can create retrieval confusion: when learners later try to recall the target word, they may retrieve the synonym instead, especially if the two words are semantically close and share other associations. The interference-theory evidence also supports this mechanism by explaining that similar memories compete during retrieval, making it harder to distinguish between the target word and the generated synonym [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The distractor-related evidence further strengthens this point by showing that semantically related options increase item difficulty and discrimination, suggesting that synonym-like features can make retrieval more error-prone [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Taken together, these mechanisms explain why synonym generation can be negative: it may create interference, encourage overgeneralization, reduce attention to the target word, and confuse retrieval between synonyms and target words. The evidence is strongest for interference and retrieval confusion, while overgeneralization is supported as a plausible secondary mechanism [N2-F2][N1-F1][N6-R1].

What the evidence says about synonym generation’s effect on recall

The evidence is mixed, but the overall pattern is not that synonym generation consistently improves recall. Instead, it appears to have mixed effects, with some studies suggesting benefits and others suggesting impairments, and the effect depends strongly on how recall is measured, the vocabulary item characteristics, and the learner group. The most directly relevant empirical source indicates that synonymy may be easier to learn than words without known synonyms, but also that synonymy is one of several interlexical factors that can reduce vocabulary acquisition [N1-F1]. This suggests that synonym generation can sometimes help, but not always.

Recall is measured in different ways in the evidence, and that matters for conclusions. The literature review describes multiple tests of word knowledge, including receptive and productive tests, and measures such as orthography, paradigmatic association, syntagmatic association, meaning and form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1]. This indicates that recall is not measured only as a simple yes/no recognition test, but also as deeper productive and contextual knowledge. The comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure also shows that retrieval practice can improve recall more than repeated exposure, especially when learners are asked to retrieve words actively rather than passively rehearse them [N3-F3]. In contrast, the synonym-generation evidence does not show a clear consistent benefit across all recall measures. Instead, it suggests that synonym generation may be more effective for some types of vocabulary knowledge than for others, and that the benefit may depend on the learner’s stage of vocabulary development [N1-F1].

Which vocabulary items and learners are most affected is also important. The evidence suggests that synonym generation may be particularly harmful when the target word has a known synonym, because learners may confuse similar words and overgeneralize usage patterns [N1-F1]. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that retrieval practice led to greater recall than repeated exposure, and that learners who were more efficient and had fewer additional diagnoses recalled more words [N3-F3]. This implies that synonym generation is likely to be less effective for learners with additional difficulties, lower efficiency, or less developed vocabulary knowledge. The literature review also notes that synonymy is especially difficult when words are closely related in meaning, and that learners may struggle with synonyms that do not share the same collocates or usage patterns [N1-F1]. This suggests that synonym generation is more harmful for words with strong semantic overlap and for learners at lower proficiency levels.

Finally, the evidence indicates that the effect of synonym generation can vary with task design and measurement. The distractor-related evidence shows that semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, which implies that synonym-related items may be harder to recall if they are presented in a retrieval context that includes plausible distractors [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The study on retrieval practice also shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental, contextualized learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2]. This suggests that synonym generation is more likely to be negative when it is incidental, when distractors are present, or when learners are not deliberately focused on retrieving the target word. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed-effect conclusion: synonym generation can help in some contexts and hurt recall in others, especially when it creates confusion, reduces attention to the target word, or introduces interference during retrieval [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1].

Contextual conditions that make synonym generation beneficial or harmful

Synonym generation can be beneficial under some conditions and harmful under others, with task design, time pressure, feedback, proficiency, and language stage all playing a key role. The evidence suggests that synonym generation is most useful when it supports deeper encoding and when learners have prior vocabulary knowledge that can be leveraged to infer meaning. The literature review states that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words without known synonyms, and that prior vocabulary knowledge can help learners acquire new words because increased vocabulary size makes more words likely to have known synonyms [N1-F1]. This implies that synonym generation is beneficial when learners are at a later stage of vocabulary development and when the target word already has semantic or associative connections to known vocabulary.

In contrast, synonym generation is harmful when the task is incidental, when there is high semantic overlap between the target word and the synonym, or when learners are not given sufficient feedback. The evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure shows that retrieval practice improves recall more than repeated exposure, especially for children with hearing loss [N3-F3]. This suggests that synonym generation can be less effective when learners are not actively retrieving the target word and when the task is passive rather than intentional. The comparative evidence also notes that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental, contextualized learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2]. So synonym generation is likely to be harmful when it is used in incidental or shallow vocabulary contexts, and beneficial when it is paired with retrieval practice or intentional study.

Task design matters because the way items are presented affects recall. The distractor-related evidence shows that semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, which implies that synonym-like distractors can make retrieval harder [N6-R1][N6-R3]. This means synonym generation is harmful when test items are designed with plausible distractors, because learners may confuse synonyms with target words during retrieval. Conversely, if the task is structured to avoid distracting features and to focus on the target word itself, synonym generation may be more beneficial [N6-R4]. Time pressure also appears relevant: the evidence on retrieval practice shows that retrieval benefits are more apparent after a retention interval, but the same evidence does not explicitly address time pressure during generation. Still, the general logic of interference theory suggests that synonym generation may be more harmful when learners are rushed or forced to produce multiple synonyms without adequate processing time [N2-F2].

Feedback is another important contextual factor. The evidence on vocabulary learning and retrieval practice shows that retrieval practice improves recall, and that retrieval benefits are influenced by whether learners are given feedback or whether they are simply asked to recall [N3-R2][N3-F3]. While the synonym-generation evidence here does not directly address feedback, the broader retrieval literature suggests that synonym generation may be harmful when learners receive no feedback or when they are only exposed to synonyms without being corrected. In contrast, synonym generation can be beneficial when it is part of a feedback-rich, intentional learning sequence [N3-R2].

Learners’ proficiency and language stage matter substantially. The literature review notes that synonymy is especially difficult when words are closely related in meaning, and that less advanced learners are unlikely to try to learn words with similar meanings [N1-F1]. This supports the conclusion that synonym generation is harmful for lower-proficiency learners and for words that are semantically dense. The study on children with hearing loss also shows that learners who were more efficient recalled more words, implying that synonym generation may be more harmful for learners who are inefficient or have additional learning difficulties [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that synonym generation is more beneficial as vocabulary knowledge grows, because learners with larger vocabularies are more likely to have known synonyms to draw on [N1-F1].

Overall, synonym generation is beneficial when it is intentional, paired with retrieval practice, and used in contexts where learners have prior vocabulary knowledge that can support semantic inference. It is harmful when the task is incidental, when there is high semantic overlap between synonyms and target words, when distractors are present, and when learners are lower in proficiency or efficiency [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Limits of the evidence and gaps in the research base

The evidence base is limited and uneven, with a mix of original studies and replications, but the available sources do not show a large number of direct synonym-generation replications. The most directly relevant empirical source is a literature review rather than a replication study, and the review notes that little research has investigated the effects of synonymy on vocabulary learning [N1-F1]. The evidence also includes a study on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure that is described as the first study of its kind for children with hearing loss [N3-F3], which suggests that the synonym-generation literature is relatively sparse and that many studies are still exploratory rather than cumulative. The search results also include a broader review on vocabulary learning strategies, a meta-analysis on technology-assisted vocabulary learning, and a study on vocabulary instruction, but none of these directly replicate synonym-generation effects [N1-R5][N5-R5][N4-R4]. This implies that the evidence is not yet strong enough to support a robust, replicated conclusion about synonym generation’s effect on recall.

Several populations and vocabulary domains are underrepresented. The available evidence focuses primarily on L2 vocabulary learning, with one study specifically on children with hearing loss and another on children with language impairment [N1-R4][N4-R1]. However, the sources do not provide much evidence on adult learners, on students with other learning differences, or on non-L2 vocabulary domains such as academic vocabulary or vocabulary in different language families. The study on children with hearing loss is useful, but it is not generalizable to all learners, and the synonym-generation literature is still mainly focused on incidental and intentional vocabulary learning rather than on vocabulary across reading, speaking, listening, or writing [N1-R4][N3-R2]. This limits the ability to draw broad conclusions about synonym generation across populations.

Study limitations prevent strong conclusions. One major limitation is that recall is measured in different ways across the evidence, including orthography, meaning, form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1], which makes comparisons difficult. The evidence also shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2], which implies that synonym-generation effects may be confounded by task intent rather than by generation itself. The distractor-related evidence further suggests that item difficulty and discrimination depend on semantically related or orthographically similar options [N6-R1][N6-R3], so recall outcomes may be influenced by test design rather than by synonym generation alone. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that additional diagnoses and learning efficiency were important predictors of recall, indicating that learner characteristics can moderate effects [N3-F3]. These limitations mean that many observed effects may be due to task design, measurement, or individual differences rather than synonym generation per se.

Overall, the evidence base is small, mixed, and methodologically uneven. There are few direct synonym-generation replications, and the literature is underrepresented for many learner populations and vocabulary domains. At the same time, the evidence shows that synonym generation can be beneficial or harmful depending on context, which makes it difficult to draw a single strong conclusion [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

The distractor-related evidence further suggests that item difficulty and discrimination depend on semantically related or orthographically similar options [N6-R1][N6-R3], so recall outcomes may be influenced by test design rather than by synonym generation alone. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that additional diagnoses and learning efficiency were important predictors of recall, indicating that learner characteristics can moderate effects [N3-F3]. These limitations mean many observed effects may be due to task design, measurement, or individual differences rather than synonym generation per se.

## Bottom line

Synonym generation can influence recall in early L2 vocabulary learning, but the effect is mixed. It can help when learners have prior vocabulary knowledge, when the task is intentional, and when retrieval is emphasized; it can hurt recall when there is high semantic overlap, when learners are less proficient, when distractors make retrieval confusing, and when the task is incidental or passive [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The main reasons for negative effects are interference from overgeneralization or overlearning, reduced attention to the target word during generation, and confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval [N2-F2][N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Overall, synonym generation is not a simple fix for vocabulary learning; its impact depends heavily on task design, learner characteristics, and the learning stage [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F3].

Mechanisms explaining negative effects of synonym generation

The evidence points to several theoretical pathways by which synonym generation can hurt recall: interference, reduced attention to target words, and confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval. First, interference theory explains why similar memories compete and make recall harder. The core idea is that previously learned information can interfere with new learning or with retrieval of previously learned information, either proactively or retroactively. This framework is directly relevant because synonym generation introduces semantically related material, which can create interference effects when the generated synonym overlaps with the target word’s meaning or with other previously learned vocabulary. The evidence also notes that interference effects can be disruptive and that susceptibility to interference can vary with age and memory processes, suggesting that synonym generation may interfere more when learners have less executive control or weaker encoding/consolidation processes [N2-R1][N2-F2].

Second, overgeneralization or overlearning can be a negative mechanism. The evidence emphasizes that synonymy can be difficult to learn because synonyms are semantically related and may be confused with one another. In the literature review, Webb notes that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words without known synonyms, but also that synonymy can be a source of difficulty because learners may confuse similar words, especially when they are closely related in meaning [N1-F1]. The review also points out that synonymy is one of several interlexical factors that can reduce vocabulary acquisition, partly because synonyms may be substituted effectively in some contexts but not in others, which can lead to overgeneralization of usage [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that synonym generation can hurt recall not only because of interference, but because learners may overlearn or generalize patterns that do not generalize correctly across contexts.

Third, reduced attention to target words during generation appears plausible. The evidence suggests that when learners are asked to generate synonyms, they may shift attention away from the target word itself. The review notes that synonymy is often learned as a later-stage phenomenon, and that teachers are unlikely to teach pairs of unknown synonyms together because it is confusing for learners [N1-F1]. This implies that synonym generation may be less effective when it is not paired with explicit attention to the target word’s meaning, form, or usage. In addition, the comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure suggests that retrieval practice can be more effective than repeated exposure because it forces learners to engage with the material actively, which implies that passive or synonym-generating tasks may fail to maintain attention at the target word level [N3-F3].

Fourth, confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval is a central mechanism. The literature review explicitly states that learners are more likely to confuse words that are similar in meaning than words that do not have close semantic links [N1-F1]. This directly supports the idea that synonym generation can create retrieval confusion: when learners later try to recall the target word, they may retrieve the synonym instead, especially if the two words are semantically close and share other associations. The interference-theory evidence also supports this mechanism by explaining that similar memories compete during retrieval, making it harder to distinguish between the target word and the generated synonym [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The distractor-related evidence further strengthens this point by showing that semantically related options increase item difficulty and discrimination, suggesting that synonym-like features can make retrieval more error-prone [N6-R1][N6-R3].

Taken together, these mechanisms explain why synonym generation can be negative: it may create interference, encourage overgeneralization, reduce attention to the target word, and confuse retrieval between synonyms and target words. The evidence is strongest for interference and retrieval confusion, while overgeneralization is supported as a plausible secondary mechanism [N2-F2][N1-F1][N6-R1].

What the evidence says about synonym generation’s effect on recall

The evidence is mixed, but the overall pattern is not that synonym generation consistently improves recall. Instead, it appears to have mixed effects, with some studies suggesting benefits and others suggesting impairments, and the effect depends strongly on how recall is measured, the vocabulary item characteristics, and the learner group. The most directly relevant empirical source indicates that synonymy may be easier to learn than words without known synonyms, but also that synonymy is one of several interlexical factors that can reduce vocabulary acquisition [N1-F1]. This suggests that synonym generation can sometimes help, but not always.

Recall is measured in different ways in the evidence, and that matters for conclusions. The literature review describes multiple tests of word knowledge, including receptive and productive tests, and measures such as orthography, paradigmatic association, syntagmatic association, meaning and form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1]. This indicates that recall is not measured only as a simple yes/no recognition test, but also as deeper productive and contextual knowledge. The comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure also shows that retrieval practice can improve recall more than repeated exposure, especially when learners are asked to retrieve words actively rather than passively rehearse them [N3-F3]. In contrast, the synonym-generation evidence does not show a clear consistent benefit across all recall measures. Instead, it suggests that synonym generation may be more effective for some types of vocabulary knowledge than for others, and that the benefit may depend on the learner’s stage of vocabulary development [N1-F1].

Which vocabulary items and learners are most affected is also important. The evidence suggests that synonym generation may be particularly harmful when the target word has a known synonym, because learners may confuse similar words and overgeneralize usage patterns [N1-F1]. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that retrieval practice led to greater recall than repeated exposure, and that learners who were more efficient and had fewer additional diagnoses recalled more words [N3-F3]. This implies that synonym generation is likely to be less effective for learners with additional difficulties, lower efficiency, or less developed vocabulary knowledge. The literature review also notes that synonymy is especially difficult when words are closely related in meaning, and that learners may struggle with synonyms that do not share the same collocates or usage patterns [N1-F1]. This suggests that synonym generation is more harmful for words with strong semantic overlap and for learners at lower proficiency levels.

Finally, the evidence indicates that the effect of synonym generation can vary with task design and measurement. The distractor-related evidence shows that semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, which implies that synonym-related items may be harder to recall if they are presented in a retrieval context that includes plausible distractors [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The study on retrieval practice also shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental, contextualized learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2]. This suggests that synonym generation is more likely to be negative when it is incidental, when distractors are present, or when learners are not deliberately focused on retrieving the target word. Overall, the evidence supports a mixed-effect conclusion: synonym generation can help in some contexts and hurt recall in others, especially when it creates confusion, reduces attention to the target word, or introduces interference during retrieval [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1].

Contextual conditions that make synonym generation beneficial or harmful

Synonym generation can be beneficial under some conditions and harmful under others, with task design, time pressure, feedback, proficiency, and language stage all playing a key role. The evidence suggests that synonym generation is most useful when it supports deeper encoding and when learners have prior vocabulary knowledge that can be leveraged to infer meaning. The literature review states that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words without known synonyms, and that prior vocabulary knowledge can help learners acquire new words because increased vocabulary size makes more words likely to have known synonyms [N1-F1]. This implies that synonym generation is beneficial when learners are at a later stage of vocabulary development and when the target word already has semantic or associative connections to known vocabulary.

In contrast, synonym generation is harmful when the task is incidental, when there is high semantic overlap between the target word and the synonym, or when learners are not given sufficient feedback. The evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure shows that retrieval practice improves recall more than repeated exposure, especially for children with hearing loss [N3-F3]. This suggests that synonym generation can be less effective when learners are not actively retrieving the target word and when the task is passive rather than intentional. The comparative evidence also notes that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental, contextualized learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2]. So synonym generation is likely to be harmful when it is used in incidental or shallow vocabulary contexts, and beneficial when it is paired with retrieval practice or intentional study.

Task design matters because the way items are presented affects recall. The distractor-related evidence shows that semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, which implies that synonym-like distractors can make retrieval harder [N6-R1][N6-R3]. This means synonym generation is harmful when test items are designed with plausible distractors, because learners may confuse synonyms with target words during retrieval. Conversely, if the task is structured to avoid distracting features and to focus on the target word itself, synonym generation may be more beneficial [N6-R4]. Time pressure also appears relevant: the evidence on retrieval practice shows that retrieval benefits are more apparent after a retention interval, but the same evidence does not explicitly address time pressure during generation. Still, the general logic of interference theory suggests that synonym generation may be more harmful when learners are rushed or forced to produce multiple synonyms without adequate processing time [N2-F2].

Feedback is another important contextual factor. The evidence on vocabulary learning and retrieval practice shows that retrieval practice improves recall, and that retrieval benefits are influenced by whether learners are given feedback or whether they are simply asked to recall [N3-R2][N3-F3]. While the synonym-generation evidence here does not directly address feedback, the broader retrieval literature suggests that synonym generation may be harmful when learners receive no feedback or when they are only exposed to synonyms without being corrected. In contrast, synonym generation can be beneficial when it is part of a feedback-rich, intentional learning sequence [N3-R2].

Learners’ proficiency and language stage matter substantially. The literature review notes that synonymy is especially difficult when words are closely related in meaning, and that less advanced learners are unlikely to try to learn words with similar meanings [N1-F1]. This supports the conclusion that synonym generation is harmful for lower-proficiency learners and for words that are semantically dense. The study on children with hearing loss also shows that learners who were more efficient recalled more words, implying that synonym generation may be more harmful for learners who are inefficient or have additional learning difficulties [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that synonym generation is more beneficial as vocabulary knowledge grows, because learners with larger vocabularies are more likely to have known synonyms to draw on [N1-F1].

Overall, synonym generation is beneficial when it is intentional, paired with retrieval practice, and used in contexts where learners have prior vocabulary knowledge that can support semantic inference. It is harmful when the task is incidental, when there is high semantic overlap between synonyms and target words, when distractors are present, and when learners are lower in proficiency or efficiency [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3].

Limits of the evidence and gaps in the research base

The evidence base is limited and uneven, with a mix of original studies and replications, but the available sources do not show a large number of direct synonym-generation replications. The most directly relevant empirical source is a literature review rather than a replication study, and the review notes that little research has investigated the effects of synonymy on vocabulary learning [N1-F1]. The search results also include a broader review on vocabulary learning strategies, a meta-analysis on technology-assisted vocabulary learning, and a study on vocabulary instruction, but none of these directly replicate synonym-generation effects [N1-R5][N5-R5][N4-R4]. The study on children with hearing loss is useful, but it is not generalizable to all learners, and the synonym-generation literature is still mainly focused on incidental and intentional vocabulary learning rather than on vocabulary across reading, speaking, listening, or writing [N1-R4][N3-R2]. This limits the ability to draw broad conclusions about synonym generation across populations.

Study limitations prevent strong conclusions. One major limitation is that recall is measured in different ways across the evidence, including orthography, meaning, form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1], which makes comparisons difficult. The evidence also shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2], which implies that synonym-generation effects may be confounded by task intent rather than by generation itself. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that additional diagnoses and learning efficiency were important predictors of recall, indicating that learner characteristics can moderate effects [N3-F3]. # Integrated explanation of how synonym generation influences recall and why it can be negative

## Overall effect: mixed, not consistently positive or negative

The evidence suggests that synonym generation does not consistently improve recall in early second language (L2) vocabulary learning. Instead, the effect is mixed: synonym generation can help in some contexts and hurt recall in others. The most directly relevant source states that synonymy may be easier to learn than words without known synonyms, but also that synonymy is one of several interlexical factors that can reduce vocabulary acquisition [N1-F1]. That means synonym generation can sometimes be useful, but it is not a universal booster of recall. The comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure also reinforces this: retrieval practice led to greater recall than repeated exposure, especially for children with hearing loss [N3-F3]. In other words, synonym generation is likely to be beneficial when paired with active retrieval, but harmful when it is passive or incidental.

## Why synonym generation can hurt recall: the main mechanisms

There are three main reasons synonym generation can be negative.

### 1) Interference from overgeneralization or overlearning

Interference theory provides a central explanation. The evidence notes that previously learned information can interfere with new learning or with retrieval, either proactively or retroactively [N2-F2]. In synonym generation, this means semantically related material can create interference when the generated synonym overlaps with the target word’s meaning or with other vocabulary. The literature review explicitly states that learners are more likely to confuse words that are similar in meaning than words that do not have close semantic links [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that synonym generation can hurt recall because learners may overgeneralize or overlearn patterns that do not generalize correctly across contexts.

### 2) Reduced attention to target words during generation

The evidence suggests that synonym generation may reduce attention to the target word itself. The literature review notes that synonymy is often learned as a later-stage phenomenon and that teachers are unlikely to teach pairs of unknown synonyms together because it is confusing for learners [N1-F1]. This implies that synonym generation may be less effective when it is not paired with explicit attention to the target word’s meaning, form, or usage. In addition, the evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure shows that retrieval practice improves recall more than repeated exposure because it forces learners to engage with the material actively [N3-F3]. That suggests that passive or synonym-generating tasks may fail to maintain attention at the target word level.

### 3) Confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval

Confusion during retrieval is one of the clearest negative effects. The literature review says learners are more likely to confuse words that are similar in meaning than words that do not have close semantic links [N1-F1]. The interference-theory evidence also supports this by explaining that similar memories compete during retrieval, making it harder to distinguish between the target word and the generated synonym [N2-R3][N2-R4]. The distractor-related evidence further strengthens this point: semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, which suggests that synonym-like features can make retrieval more error-prone [N6-R1][N6-R3]. So synonym generation can hurt recall because learners may retrieve the synonym instead of the target word, especially when the two are closely related.

## When synonym generation is useful versus when it is harmful

Synonym generation is useful when it supports deeper encoding and when learners have prior vocabulary knowledge that can be leveraged to infer meaning. The literature review states that learning synonyms for known words may be easier than learning words without known synonyms, and that prior vocabulary knowledge can help learners acquire new words because increased vocabulary size makes more words likely to have known synonyms [N1-F1]. That implies synonym generation is beneficial when learners are at a later stage of vocabulary development and when the target word already has semantic or associative connections to known vocabulary.

In contrast, synonym generation is harmful when the task is incidental, when there is high semantic overlap between the target word and the synonym, or when learners are not given sufficient feedback. The evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental, contextualized learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2]. That suggests synonym generation is more likely to be harmful in incidental or shallow vocabulary contexts. The distractor-related evidence also shows that semantically related or orthographically similar options increase item difficulty and discrimination, meaning synonym generation is more harmful when test items are designed with plausible distractors [N6-R1][N6-R3]. In short, synonym generation is beneficial when it is intentional and paired with retrieval practice; it is harmful when the task is incidental, when there are strong semantic overlaps, and when distractors make retrieval confusing.

## Role of task design, time pressure, and feedback

Task design matters a lot. The evidence shows that retrieval benefits are more apparent when learners are asked to retrieve words actively rather than passively rehearse them [N3-F3]. The distractor-related evidence further shows that item difficulty and discrimination depend on semantically related or orthographically similar options, so synonym generation is more harmful when items are designed with plausible distractors [N6-R1][N6-R3]. This means synonym generation is likely to be negative when test items are not carefully structured to avoid confusing features.

Time pressure may also play a role. While the evidence does not explicitly address time pressure during generation, the broader logic of interference theory suggests that synonym generation may be more harmful when learners are rushed or forced to produce multiple synonyms without adequate processing time [N2-F2]. This implies that synonym generation is more likely to hurt recall when it is done under time pressure rather than when learners can process the target word carefully.

Feedback is another important contextual factor. The evidence on retrieval practice shows that retrieval benefits are influenced by whether learners are given feedback or whether they are simply asked to recall [N3-R2][N3-F3]. Although the synonym-generation evidence here does not directly address feedback, the broader retrieval literature suggests that synonym generation may be harmful when learners receive no feedback or when they are only exposed to synonyms without being corrected. In contrast, synonym generation can be beneficial when it is part of a feedback-rich, intentional learning sequence [N3-R2].

## How learners’ proficiency and language stage matter

Learners’ proficiency and language stage are strongly related to how synonym generation affects recall. The literature review notes that synonymy is especially difficult when words are closely related in meaning, and that less advanced learners are unlikely to try to learn words with similar meanings [N1-F1]. This supports the conclusion that synonym generation is harmful for lower-proficiency learners and for words that are semantically dense. The study on children with hearing loss also shows that learners who were more efficient recalled more words, implying that synonym generation may be more harmful for learners who are inefficient or have additional learning difficulties [N3-F3]. The evidence also implies that synonym generation is more beneficial as vocabulary knowledge grows, because learners with larger vocabularies are more likely to have known synonyms to draw on [N1-F1].

## What the evidence says about recall measurement and conclusions

Recall is measured in different ways in the evidence, and that affects conclusions. The literature review describes multiple tests of word knowledge, including receptive and productive tests, and measures such as orthography, paradigmatic association, syntagmatic association, meaning and form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1]. This means recall is not measured only as a simple yes/no recognition test, but also as deeper productive and contextual knowledge. The comparative evidence on retrieval practice versus repeated exposure also shows that retrieval practice can improve recall more than repeated exposure, especially when learners are asked to retrieve words actively rather than passively rehearse them [N3-F3]. In contrast, the synonym-generation evidence does not show a clear consistent benefit across all recall measures. Instead, it suggests that synonym generation may be more effective for some types of vocabulary knowledge than for others, and that the benefit may depend on the learner’s stage of vocabulary development [N1-F1].

## Which vocabulary items and learners are most affected

Some vocabulary items and learners are more likely to be affected by synonym generation than others. The evidence suggests that synonym generation may be particularly harmful when the target word has a known synonym, because learners may confuse similar words and overgeneralize usage patterns [N1-F1]. It is also more harmful for words that are closely related in meaning, and for learners at lower proficiency levels [N1-F1]. The study on children with hearing loss found that learners who were more efficient recalled more words, implying that synonym generation may be more harmful for learners who are inefficient or have additional learning difficulties [N3-F3]. So the most affected vocabulary items are those with strong semantic overlap, and the most affected learners are lower-proficiency learners and those with additional learning challenges.

## Limits of the evidence and gaps in the research base

The evidence base is limited and uneven. The available sources include original studies and replications, but there are not many direct synonym-generation replications in the evidence provided [N1-F1]. The literature review is itself a review rather than a replication study, and it notes that little research has investigated the effects of synonymy on vocabulary learning [N1-F1]. This implies that the evidence is still sparse and that many studies are exploratory rather than cumulative. The evidence also includes a broader review on vocabulary learning strategies, a meta-analysis on technology-assisted vocabulary learning, and a study on vocabulary instruction, but none of these directly replicate synonym-generation effects [N1-R5][N5-R5][N4-R4]. This means the conclusions are still tentative.

Several populations and vocabulary domains are underrepresented. The evidence focuses primarily on L2 vocabulary learning, with one study specifically on children with hearing loss and another on children with language impairment [N1-R4][N4-R1]. However, the sources do not provide much evidence on adult learners, on students with other learning differences, or on non-L2 vocabulary domains such as academic vocabulary or vocabulary in different language families [N4-R4]. The study on children with hearing loss is useful, but it is not generalizable to all learners, and the synonym-generation literature is still mainly focused on incidental and intentional vocabulary learning rather than on vocabulary across reading, speaking, listening, or writing [N1-R4][N3-R2]. This limits the ability to draw broad conclusions about synonym generation across populations.

Study limitations prevent strong conclusions. One major limitation is that recall is measured in different ways across the evidence, including orthography, meaning, form, and grammatical functions [N1-F1], which makes comparisons difficult. The evidence also shows that retrieval benefits are less pronounced during incidental learning than during intentional exercises [N3-R2], which implies that synonym-generation effects may be confounded by task intent rather than by generation itself. The distractor-related evidence further suggests that item difficulty and discrimination depend on semantically related or orthographically similar options [N6-R1][N6-R3], so recall outcomes may be influenced by test design rather than by synonym generation alone. In addition, the study on children with hearing loss found that additional diagnoses and learning efficiency were important predictors of recall, indicating that learner characteristics can moderate effects [N3-F3]. These limitations mean many observed effects may be due to task design, measurement, or individual differences rather than synonym generation per se.

## Bottom line

Synonym generation can influence recall in early L2 vocabulary learning, but the effect is mixed. It can help when learners have prior vocabulary knowledge, when the task is intentional, and when retrieval is emphasized; it can hurt recall when there is high semantic overlap, when learners are less proficient, when distractors make retrieval confusing, and when the task is incidental or passive [N1-F1][N3-F3][N6-R1][N6-R3]. The main reasons for negative effects are interference from overgeneralization or overlearning, reduced attention to the target word during generation, and confusion between synonyms and target words during retrieval [N2-F2][N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. Overall, synonym generation is not a simple fix for vocabulary learning; its impact depends heavily on task design, learner characteristics, and the learning stage [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-F3].

There are three main reasons synonym generation can be negative.

Interference theory provides a central explanation. The evidence suggests that synonym generation may reduce attention to the target word itself.
